**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> EasyContext is an open-source toolkit that addresses the challenge of extending language model context windows to extreme sizes—up to 1 million tokens—using accessible hardware. It enables training Llama-2-7B with a 700K context on just 8 A100 GPUs and Llama-2-13B with a 1M context on 16 A100 GPUs, using full finetuning, full attention, and full sequence length without approximations. The toolkit combines existing optimization techniques, including sequence parallelism (Ring Attention, Dist Flash Attention, and Ulysses), DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 offload, Flash Attention with fused cross-entropy, and activation checkpointing, integrating them through a concise training script under 200 lines. It works by gradually increasing the RoPE base frequency to 1B during training, allowing models trained at 512K sequences to generalize to nearly 1M tokens. Researchers and engineers working on long-context LLMs, particularly those with limited compute resources, will find this useful for demystifying and reproducing extreme context-length training. The project also provides evaluation tools for needle-in-a-haystack retrieval and perplexity benchmarking on long documents.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Step-Audio-R1 is an audio reasoning model from StepFun that addresses the "inverted scaling" problem in audio language models, where extended Chain-of-Thought reasoning paradoxically degrades performance. It introduces Modality-Grounded Reasoning Distillation (MGRD), an iterative training framework that shifts reasoning from textual surrogates (analyzing transcripts) to genuine acoustic analysis, enabling the model to benefit from test-time compute scaling. Built on a Qwen2 audio encoder and Qwen2.5 32B LLM decoder, Step-Audio-R1 surpasses Gemini 2.5 Pro and performs comparably to Gemini 3 across audio benchmarks. The repository also includes Step-Audio-R1.1 (Realtime), which adds a Dual-Brain Architecture for low-latency interactive spoken dialogue with "mind-paced speaking," and Step-Audio-R1.5, which incorporates Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback to better preserve prosodic naturalness and emotional continuity in long-turn audio dialogue. The codebase provides vLLM-based inference code, Gradio demos, model checkpoints on HuggingFace and ModelScope, and three open-source evaluation benchmarks (step_caption, step_spqa, step_dialogue_understanding). Researchers, developers, and practitioners building voice-driven AI applications—including conversational agents, audio analysis tools, and real-time speech interfaces—would benefit from this work.

**Product Description Text**:
> NVIDIA Object Oriented Agents (NOOA) is a model-agnostic Python framework that unifies agent construction around native Python classes, replacing the fragmented prompt/tool/workflow abstractions found in most agent libraries. Developers define agents as subclasses of `Agent`, with typed fields for state, ordinary methods for deterministic logic, and `...`-bodied async methods that the runtime hands to an LLM, whose docstrings serve as prompts and whose type annotations define I/O contracts. Agents execute Python in a Jupyter-style REPL, calling other class methods directly rather than relying on separate tool-schema definitions, which enables typed inputs/outputs, auto-retry, and live-object argument passing. The framework is aimed at Python developers building reliable, testable AI agents and supports any LiteLLM-compatible model, including hosted services (Anthropic, OpenAI) and local runtimes (Ollama, vLLM). Optional sub-packages extend the core with a CLI and trace viewer (`nooa-cli`), long-term memory (`nooa-memory`), and a Harbor benchmark runner (`nooa-bench`), with installation managed via `uv` or `pip`. Because agents execute LLM-generated code, NOOA is positioned as research software intended to run inside OS-level sandboxes such as containers or NVIDIA OpenShell.

> Wan-Move is a NeurIPS 2025 research project from Alibaba (ali-vilab) that extends the Wan2.1 image-to-video model with fine-grained, point-level motion control without requiring architectural changes or extra motion modules. The method propagates the first frame's features along user-specified point trajectories to guide video generation, producing 5-second 480p videos with state-of-the-art motion controllability comparable to commercial systems such as Kling 1.5 Pro's Motion Brush. Dense point trajectories enable precise, region-level control of object motion in single and multi-object scenes, and a Gradio demo lets creators draw trajectories interactively. The release also ships MoveBench, a curated benchmark with diverse content, longer video durations, and high-quality trajectory annotations. Backbone: Wan-I2V-14B; framework: PyTorch (>=2.4.0); supporting tools include CoTracker, umt5-xxl, and HuggingFace; acceleration via FSDP and xDiT USP for multi-GPU inference; ComfyUI and Wan2GP wrappers support low-VRAM usage. License: Apache-2.0.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> rCM introduces a novel framework for scaling up continuous-time consistency distillation methods, such as sCM and MeanFlow, to large-scale video diffusion models. The work utilizes a Score-Regularized approach combined with JVP-based diffusion distillation to enhance both the quality and diversity of generated videos. A key innovation is the forward–reverse divergence joint distillation, which effectively complements traditional distillation methods by addressing the quality bottleneck in consistency models. Furthermore, rCM provides an open-sourced FlashAttention-2 Jacobian-vector product kernel, enabling efficient parallelization for large-scale training. This methodology allows for state-of-the-art video generation in only a few steps, significantly improving generation efficiency.

It features a prompt-based data synthesis agent that autonomously generates grounded, uncertain QA pairs using fuzzing and context injection strategies, with multi-stage validation ensuring question quality and difficulty. > humanizer-cli is a terminal-based tool that helps writers and editors identify 33 common patterns of AI-generated text, drawn from Wikipedia's "Signs of AI writing" catalog. It solves the problem of detecting and revising the mechanical tells of language model output—em dashes in place of commas, "not just X, it's Y" constructions, padded phrasing, emoji in headings, and similar habits—without sending any content to a remote service. Key features include a `patterns` command that lists every tell grouped by section, a `show <n>` command for detailed before-and-after examples, a `search` command for keyword lookup, and a `check <file>` command that scans drafts and reports matches for 13 of the 33 patterns that can be caught mechanically. A `prompt` command exports the full skill prompt and an optional draft to the clipboard for use with any chat-based rewriter, removing the need for an API key. The technology stack is deliberately minimal: a single C binary (under 100 KB on Windows x64) that has zero runtime dependencies, wrapped in a Node.js launcher for `npx`/`npm install -g` distribution. Writers, editors, journalists, and anyone concerned about AI-text fingerprints would find it useful as a self-contained, offline editing aid.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> claude-watch is a Claude Code skill (also installable on claude.ai and Codex) that lets Claude actually watch a video instead of guessing from titles or transcripts. Users paste a YouTube/Loom/TikTok link or a local file, and the skill downloads it via yt-dlp, extracts frames with ffmpeg, pulls a transcript (native captions first, Whisper API as fallback), and feeds both into Claude's context so it can answer grounded in real visual and audio evidence. Its standout feature is scene-change frame extraction, which captures one frame per detected cut rather than a uniform tick, keeping token usage bounded by the number of shots rather than video length. A 0-10s "hook microscope" runs a denser 2 fps pass plus word-level Whisper on the opening seconds, where videos earn or lose viewer attention, producing a structured `report.md` with explicit fill markers for TL;DR, key moments, quotable lines, and entities. Optional Obsidian auto-save stages the report into a vault directory and opens it via the `obsidian://` URL scheme, turning watched videos into connected wiki entries without copy-paste. The stack is deliberately minimal: yt-dlp for ingestion, ffmpeg for frame and audio extraction, Groq or OpenAI Whisper for transcription, and Python scripts orchestrated as a Claude skill — no server, no database, zero config to start. The audience is creators reverse-engineering viral hooks, developers debugging screen-recorded bug repros, and researchers or knowledge workers who want to sum

It enables users to query any existing PostgreSQL schema through plain English prompts, without requiring schema modifications or assumptions about table structure. The server enforces read-only access for safety, supports automatic streaming of large result sets, and handles PostgreSQL case sensitivity, including mixed-case table and column names. Results can be returned in table, JSON, or CSV formats, with optional free-text search across all text columns. Built in Go, PGMCP integrates with MCP-compatible clients like Cursor, Claude Desktop, and VS Code, and optionally leverages OpenAI (or local LLMs via Ollama) for AI-powered SQL generation with graceful error recovery. The method allows users to super-resolve a small set of keyframes and then propagate these priors across the entire video sequence while maintaining adherence to the original low-resolution motion. It employs a keyframe-conditioned latent-pixel two-stage training pipeline to fuse low-resolution and high-resolution latents, ensuring robust cross-space propagation. During inference, the model supports flexible keyframe selection and reference-free guidance for superior restoration quality. Experiments demonstrate improved temporal consistency and strong restoration, outperforming baselines on key video quality benchmarks. This approach establishes SparkVSR as a generic, keyframe-driven framework applicable to various video processing tasks.

**Product Description Text**:
> Tree Search for LLM Agent Reinforcement Learning

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Tree-GRPO is an ICLR 2026-accepted method that replaces traditional independent chain-based rollouts with tree-search rollouts for LLM agent reinforcement learning, addressing the inefficiency and lack of process supervision in standard GRPO training. Built on ReAct step-level nodes, it performs rollout sampling over semantically well-defined search trees, delivering two key benefits: reduced rollout budget requirements and tree-based process supervision signals. Experimental results demonstrate that Tree-GRPO achieves superior performance over chain-based GRPO across single-hop QA (NQ, TriviaQA, PopQA) and multi-hop QA benchmarks (HotpotQA, 2Wiki, MuSiQue, Bamboogle) using only a quarter of the rollout budget, with consistent improvements across Qwen2.5 (1.5B–14B) and Llama3.2-3B model families. The framework targets researchers and engineers working on LLM agent training, search-augmented generation, and retrieval-augmented reasoning systems. The technology stack is built on PyTorch 2.6, vLLM 0.8.5, and Flash Attention 2, leveraging the veRL framework for RL training and supporting both local retrieval servers (with Pyserini/FAISS-GPU) and real Bing search APIs for web-agent QA.

Platforms: Linux desktop (full pipeline), macOS Apple Silicon (transcription/labeling/sync only; capture requires Linux); Windows not supported. License: GPL-3.0.

Users provide an initial prompt and a description of desired improvements, and the tool iteratively generates, mutates, and evaluates candidate prompts using an LLM-as-judge with self-consistency as the default scoring method. It adapts the minimal GPT architecture to learn how to denoise corrupted text sequences. **Product Description Text**:
> NIGHTRUN is a Rust-based, bare-metal LLM runtime that boots from USB (x86_64 UEFI) or microSD (Raspberry Pi 5) and serves a quantized model directly on the framebuffer, with no host operating system, network stack, or browser involved. It targets users who need an offline, deterministic, fully local inference environment, ranging from privacy-conscious individuals running a private terminal on commodity hardware, to embedded/edge developers who want a self-contained image, to AI researchers validating that hand-written quantized kernels remain bit-identical to llama.cpp across model families. The stack is a single UEFI application using `no_std` Rust, with custom GGUF conversion into a sealed `.nrm` container, CRC-32 streaming verification, multi-core inference via firmware MP services, and hand-written AVX2+FMA+F16C (x86_64) or NEON (Pi 5) kernels for Q8_0, Q4_K and Q6_K weights used in place, plus a custom framebuffer chat UI with caret editing, scrollback, and live tok/s stats. Supported models include Llama 3.2 (1B/3B), Granite 4.1 3B, and Qwen3 4B, each with its tokenizer and chat template pinned against official Hugging Face fixtures. Storage is intentionally sealed after model load so the generation loop can never touch disk, making decode latency predictable and bounded by memory bandwidth. The included installer builds the bootable image, verifies the model via pinned SHA-256, and flashes removable media only after explicit `FLASH /dev/sdX` confirmation.

> humanizer-stack is a two-pass pipeline for removing AI writing tells from outward-facing text, packaged as Claude Code Skills. It pairs a surface pass (vocabulary, punctuation, and phrasing fixes drawn from Wikipedia's Signs of AI writing plus a 3.2M-post Reddit analysis of copy tells) with a structural pass grounded in the StoryScope study, which detected AI-authored stories at 93.2% F1 using discourse-level features alone and found that span-level rewriting only reduced detection by 1.6 points. The structural pass runs six audits (theme explicitness, structural tidiness, emotion mode, reference specificity, reader engagement, and shape convergence) one at a time, since aspect-based checking recovered 95% of issues in the study's own pipeline against 68% for a combined pass. Two deterministic scanners (copy_scan.py and structural_scan.py) provide grep-able, hook-friendly checks with JSON output and strict-exit modes, while the skills themselves handle the judgment work. The target audience is writers, marketers, and developers using Claude Code who need outbound copy and short fiction that reads as though a person wrote it, aware that no tool makes text undetectable and that "show, don't tell" now functions as a machine signature. The stack is plain Python, markdown reference material, and shell installer, distributed under MIT with upstream CC BY-SA 4.0 obligations.

**Product Description Text**:
> FlowBlock is a training-free, parallel decoding framework designed to accelerate block-wise diffusion language models (dLLMs) such as LLaDA-2.x, which otherwise decode one block at a time in strict serial order. It solves the throughput bottleneck of these models by exploiting the token-to-token self-correction ability of LLaDA-2.1, treating block finality as a scheduling resource rather than a hard dependency, so downstream blocks can begin decoding from informative drafts instead of finalized predecessors. The framework introduces two mechanisms: Gated Wavefront Decoding (GWD), which uses a readiness gate to admit blocks into a bounded wavefront while jointly refining active blocks via T2T editing and committing them under a windowed block-causal mask that preserves exact frozen-prefix KV-cache reuse; and Heterogeneous Wavefront Packing (HWP), which assigns each request its own wavefront while packing all active windows into dense, shape-stable batched forwards for GPU-efficient asynchronous serving. FlowBlock achieves up to 2.95× / 4.01× higher tokens-per-second than LLaDA-2.1 / LLaDA-2.0 under batched serving, with up to 53.6% / 77.1% lower latency and comparable or improved accuracy (+1.3 points average across eight math and code benchmarks), all without retraining. It targets researchers and engineers working on efficient inference for diffusion language models, particularly in batched serving environments. The stack is Python 3.11 with PyTorch 2.8.0 (CUDA 12.x), vLLM 0

**Product Description Text**:
> Reame is a lean, CPU-first LLM inference server built on llama.cpp, designed to run useful models on cheap or free-tier hardware such as shared vCPUs and 2-core ARM boxes rather than relying on GPUs. Its core thesis is avoiding redundant computation: a persistent shared-prefix KV cache lets prompt prefixes be snapshotted to disk and reused across requests, restarts, and processes, while Palimpsest archives past generations so repetitive workloads draft future tokens at zero cost. It adds grammar-based speculative decoding ("Il Suggeritore"), a self-regulating draft model that disables itself when speculation doesn't pay, a "Conclave" mode for consensus-based best-of-N generation, and interleaved multi-user batching that shares model-weight reads across concurrent requests. An optional Redis-compatible ARCA daemon provides an exact-response cache and a fleet-wide generation corpus, and the server exposes an OpenAI-compatible REST API with streaming, sessions, and bearer auth. Reame is aimed at developers running narrow, repetitive AI workloads over their own data—document extraction, batch tagging, privacy-bound inference, SaaS features, and code completion—who need predictable, low-cost performance without GPUs. The headline result is a measured ~6× speedup and improved accuracy on a 20-question fact exam achieved by rewriting inputs into compact label:value form rather than tuning the engine, with benchmarks, negative results, and 261 isolated test cases published alongside

**Product Description Text**:
> Production-grade Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture using Open Source components

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> A production-grade Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system built on open-source components, enabling accurate, citation-backed Q&A over document corpora. It tackles the limitations of standalone LLMs—including hallucinations and outdated knowledge—by grounding responses in retrieved source material. The architecture combines dense vector search with BM25 sparse retrieval, fuses results via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, and reranks outputs using a cross-encoder (BAAI/bge-reranker-base) for higher precision. PDF ingestion is handled with multiple extraction strategies, and an interactive chat interface enables natural-language control over indexing and querying. It allows running models like Llama 70B on a single 4GB GPU, Llama 3.1 405B on 8GB, DeepSeek-V3 (671B) on ~12GB, and even the 2.8T-parameter Kimi K3 on under 4GB by streaming only the active experts in sparse MoE architectures. The library is designed for AI practitioners, researchers, and developers who want to run state-of-the-art LLMs locally without expensive enterprise hardware. Built on top of HuggingFace Transformers with optional integration of bitsandbytes and flash-attention, it supports a broad range of models including Qwen, Llama, DeepSeek, Mixtral, ChatGLM, Mistral, and Phi families.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> AnyJev turns any open LLM into a Jev-style decision model that outputs typed choices with calibrated probabilities, without fine-tuning or generated text. It addresses two core problems with raw LLM logits for decision-making: answer instability when options are reordered (fixed zero-label via rotation at L0) and untrustworthy confidence (fixed with ~100–300 labels via a closed-form linear head at L2). Key features include four levels of increasing fidelity (raw, L0, L1, L2), a rotation budget that cuts average rotations from 18 to 7.2 at certified 1% disagreement, depth truncation that often improves both accuracy and speed, and a deployment model where L2 is simply a vLLM embed server plus kilobytes of head weights. It is aimed at engineers building routing, classification, triage, and routing-style automation pipelines who need trustworthy thresholds rather than best-guess text completions. The stack is Python with vLLM or transformers backends, distributed on PyPI, and ships pretrained heads for the Qwen3 family in a 1.8–4.4 MB file per model.

> *(No brief description text provided in original record)*

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> `fast-jev-compaction` replaces lossy LLM-based context summarization in Claude Code with a deterministic pruning approach using the Typesafe Jev model. Instead of rewriting conversation history, it scores every tool call and result via Jev to decide whether to keep, truncate, or drop them—while preserving all user and assistant text verbatim and never leaving a `tool_result` without its `tool_use`. The state sent to Jev fits into configurable token budgets (25k state, 30k request) through staged reductions (input truncation, text abridgement, message collapsing, call-only folding) using a tokenizer-free character-based estimator calibrated against Jev's reported counts.

The package ships as both an npm library exposing primitives like `compactMessages`, `collectToolCalls`, `fitState`, and `buildJevRequest`, and as a Claude Code function-hook plugin (`hooks/fast-jev.ts`) that intercepts `session.compact` and falls back to the built-in summarizer on insufficient reduction or error. Requests run concurrently with batched `noul` scoring questions per tool call, and a configurable `keepThreshold` plus `reductionRatio()` helper lets callers decide when pruning is worthwhile versus keeping the original transcript.

Targeted at developers building long-running Claude Code sessions where context-window exhaustion is recurring and exact values—file paths, errors, command outputs, constraints—must survive across compactions, the library requires only a `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` and a Claude C

It is built around three guarantees that most chat-with-search interfaces do not offer: an enforced cost or token budget (every model and search call is reserved in a database ledger before it runs and settled after, so `--usd 0.50` is a hard ceiling rather than an estimate), quote-verified claims (a claim whose quote cannot be located verbatim in its source is rejected at extraction, and claims that turn out unsupported on later reading are flagged rather than silently dropped), and a local-data privacy boundary (CSV/TSV/JSON/JSONL files can be analysed without their contents ever leaving the machine, with only aggregates covering at least five rows allowed back, logged via `mole crossings`). **Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> ollama-ram-guard is a lightweight Windows watchdog that solves Ollama's lack of OS memory awareness by automatically unloading idle models when system RAM runs low, preventing situations where a forgotten model pins a 16 GB laptop near zero free memory. It uses conservative safety rules, only evicting models that are demonstrably idle (detected by observing unchanged keep-alive deadlines across polls), respecting protected models, capping unloads per cycle, and enforcing cooldown periods. The tool is a single Python file using only the standard library, requires no pip dependencies, and is installed as a Windows Scheduled Task running short polling passes rather than a persistent loop, ensuring protection survives crashes. It supports dry-run mode, JSON configuration with extensive tunables, state persistence between runs, proactive idle eviction, and a CLI fallback via `ollama stop`. Local LLM users on memory-constrained Windows machines who run Ollama as a backend would find it useful, and the codebase includes 33 mocked unit tests, a design document, and an MIT license.

Its pipeline first extracts rubrics from arXiv papers to synthesize 20,000 instances across five domains (PaperGym-20k), then applies a two-stage "teach-explore" paradigm: rubric-conditioned self-distillation (OPSD) followed by GRPO with rubric-as-reward, using the extracted rubrics twice to improve both supervision and reinforcement signals. The approach achieves only 3.7% criterion leakage (3–9× lower than existing benchmarks), delivers +4.8 to +5.6 point gains over base Qwen3 models, and reaches a 58.1% win rate against baselines while surpassing the much larger Kimi K2.6 on ResearchQA with a fine-tuned 8B model. Researchers working on automated scientific reasoning, LLM post-training, or rubric-based evaluation will find the released corpus, fine-tuned models (1B/4B/8B), and held-out benchmarks (PaperGym-Innov, PaperGym-Design) directly useful. The codebase is built on PyTorch with TRL for the OPSD stage, verl for GRPO, vLLM for inference, and includes comprehensive evaluation tooling for leakage detection, win-rate comparisons, entropy analysis, and scorer stability.

It introduces ECBench, a 2,000-instance benchmark built from the RTS-GMLC grid and real data-center profiles, where every instance is paired with a Gurobi-derived oracle optimum and scored on grid safety, computing satisfaction, economy, and efficiency. A deterministic DC power-flow verifier replays the agent's decisions hourly without calling a solver at inference, and a Feasibility-Aware GRPO (FA-GRPO) training stage turns the verifier's verdict into the reward signal. On held-out evaluation, PowerAtlas cuts summed grid violations by an order of magnitude or more across Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Falcon3-3B backbones while raising served task value to roughly 90–99%, outperforming a strong frontier baseline that still leaves 445.8 MWh of violations. The repository is intended for researchers working at the intersection of LLM reasoning, reinforcement learning, and power-systems optimization, as well as operators exploring co-scheduling of compute and grid resources. Researchers and developers working on autonomous code generation, AI-assisted software development, and agentic LLM systems will find R2E-Gym valuable for both training and benchmarking purposes. > WERM (Wiring-Encoded Recurrent Modulator) is a 302-neuron simulation built on the real adult *C. elegans* connectome from Cook et al. 2019, using a liquid time constant network that runs on the actual wiring (3,709 chemical connections, 1,105 gap junctions) rather than a random or fitted architecture. It serves two audiences: neuroscientists and ML researchers who want a reproducible, biologically grounded spiking-free model with published stimulus-response results (tail touch drives forward motion, nose touch reverses, shuffled networks fail to reproduce these asymmetries), and LLM users who want a local, privacy-preserving way to inject a "neural state" into a language model's sampling parameters. The steering layer maps worm state to temperature, top_p, repetition penalty, and a one-line system-prompt tone nudge, then forwards those settings to any OpenAI-compatible local server (Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, vLLM), keeping all inference on-device. The stack is pure Node 20+ ESM with zero runtime dependencies, a Python helper only for rebuilding the connectome from the CECT spreadsheet, and a static site (`site/`) that visualizes the model with a generative pixel worm, a connectome globe, and a to-scale genome. Everything is reproducible: parameter sweeps, reservoir benchmarks, and steering evaluations ship as runnable scripts, so reviewers can rerun the published numbers or extend them.

**Product Description Text**:
> Turn any codebase, with its docs, SQL schemas, configs, and PDFs, into a queryable knowledge graph. A /graphify skill for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and Gemini CLI: local deterministic AST parsing, every edge explained, no vector store.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Graphify solves the problem of navigating and understanding large, multi-format codebases by converting them into a queryable knowledge graph instead of forcing developers to grep through files manually. By invoking the `/graphify` skill in AI coding assistants like Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or Gemini CLI, users can map an entire project—including source code, documentation, SQL schemas, configuration files, and PDFs—into a structured graph that can be explored visually or queried programmatically.

The tool relies on local, deterministic AST parsing via tree-sitter across roughly 40 programming languages, meaning code analysis requires no LLM calls and no data leaves the user's machine. Each edge in the resulting graph is explicitly tagged as either `EXTRACTED` (directly present in the source) or `INFERRED` (resolved through graph traversal), giving users clear visibility into provenance. Output includes an interactive `graph.html` viewer, a `GRAPH_REPORT.md` summary highlighting key concepts and surprising connections, and a portable `graph.json` file for later querying, path-finding, and explanation. Unlike vector-based memory systems, Graphify builds a true traversable graph with community detection (Leiden algorithm), cross-file relationship resolution (`calls`, `imports`, `inherits`, `mixes_in`), and integration of rationale comments and ADR references.

It is aimed at developers, architects, and engineering teams working with unfamiliar or sprawling codebases who nee

> GBrain is a self-hosted brain layer for AI agents that transforms raw document retrieval into synthesized, cited answers. Built by Garry Tan as the production memory behind his OpenClaw and Hermes deployments, it manages 155,795 pages across 24,589 people and 5,340 companies with 66 autonomous cron jobs running 24/7 for ingestion, enrichment, and overnight memory consolidation.

The system combines two core capabilities: a synthesis layer that produces well-cited prose responses (rather than returning search chunks) plus explicit gap analysis noting what the brain doesn't yet know, and a self-wiring knowledge graph that extracts typed entity relationships like `works_at`, `invested_in`, and `attended` on every page write without LLM calls. This hybrid approach delivers P@5 of 49.1% and R@5 of 97.9% on a 240-page benchmark corpus, beating graph-disabled and BM25-plus-vector baselines by over 31 points.

GBrain targets individual developers wanting a personal knowledge agent, YC-style teams needing scoped shared institutional memory (each user gets a permissioned slice with zero cross-leak fuzz-tested across all read paths), and AI agent builders wiring it in as a supercharged retrieval layer for Claude Code or Codex. The stack runs on PostgreSQL via PGLite (database ready in 2 seconds, no server required), Bun, and integrates through MCP, with install paths supporting everything from a 15-minute Codex setup to a full 30-minute always-on daemon deployment.

- **Attached Keywords**: `ai-agents, python, cli, agent, context-management, memory, knowledge-base`

**Product Description Text**:
> OptMem is a lightweight, permanent memory system designed for AI coding agents like Claude Code. It solves the statelessness problem that forces agents to lose context between sessions, compactions, model switches, and vendor changes by giving them a single, append-only log of long-term facts. The system consists of a single dependency-free Python 3 script (`memo`) installed via curl, plus a 426-token Markdown prompt that any agent pastes into its `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`. From there, agents run `memo wake` at session start to read their memory and `memo note "<line>"` whenever they learn something worth keeping, with merges handled one at a time in command output rather than via background processes. Storage uses fixed-width records so position equals identity, enabling O(1) lookups that scale to a million memories (608 MB) with wake times of 0.03 seconds. Summaries form a binary tree that can be navigated with `memo zoom <a>-<b>` and rebuilt from the log alone, making the cache fully reconstructible. Search is regex-based (`memo recall`), bad summaries can be dropped with `memo forget`, and the entire memory directory can be redirected via `$MEMORY_DIR` to sync across machines or version-control. The target users are developers running long-lived AI agent workflows who need continuity without maintaining complex infrastructure or external databases.

**Product Description Text**:
> SkillRL: Evolving Agents via Recursive Skill-Augmented Reinforcement Learning

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> SkillRL addresses the inefficiency of memory-based LLM agent training by abstracting raw, noisy trajectories into a hierarchical skill library that bridges experience and policy improvement. The framework distills successful trajectories into strategic "General Skills" and "Task-Specific Skills," while failed trajectories are condensed into concise lessons, achieving 10–20% token compression compared to raw trajectory storage. A recursive skill evolution mechanism allows the skill bank to co-evolve with the agent's policy during reinforcement learning by analyzing validation failures, ensuring the knowledge base remains relevant and useful. The system supports two retrieval modes—template-based keyword matching and embedding-based semantic search using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B—allowing flexible injection of the top-k most relevant skills into agent prompts. Researchers and engineers working on LLM-based agent training, particularly those targeting decision-making benchmarks like ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search tasks, will find SkillRL useful for improving reasoning capability and sample efficiency. The stack is built on PyTorch with vLLM (v0.11.0) and FlashAttention (v2.7.4) for inference, LLaMA-Factory for SFT, and a GRPO-based trainer for RL, integrating environment packages such as alfworld, gymnasium, and stable-baselines3.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> A FastAPI-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation service that integrates Langchain with PostgreSQL/pgvector for document indexing and semantic search, organizing embeddings by file and entity identifiers rather than free-form queries. It provides asynchronous document management endpoints for adding, retrieving, querying, and deleting document chunks, with a built-in ownership scope resolved from JWT tokens so callers only access content they own. Designed primarily for LibreChat integration, the API supports file-level and entity-level (agent knowledge base) ownership, treating any file outside the caller's scope as "not found" rather than "found but refused" to avoid existence leakage. The service uses pgvector for vector storage and supports deployment via Docker Compose with separate configurations for the API and database. Notable features include authorization checks applied before ranking in queries, owner-aware deletion that requires the entity_id used during upload, and a documented upgrade path for clients to avoid orphaning entity-owned files. The technology stack comprises Python, FastAPI, Langchain, PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension, and OpenAI embeddings (with proxy/base URL support), deployable through Docker or local virtual environments.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Second Brain solves the fragmentation problem of AI tool usage: when you split work between Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, and other assistants, your context, including projects, decisions, and preferences, gets lost between sessions, forcing you to re-explain yourself repeatedly. It provides a single, persistent memory layer that every MCP-compatible AI client can read and write to, so context follows you across tools instead of staying trapped in one platform. The system runs as a self-hosted Worker in your own Cloudflare account (free tier), keeping memory ownership with the user rather than any AI vendor. Key features include semantic recall via vector search, a connected memory graph with `hops`-based traversal, integrations for Notion, Google/Outlook/iCloud calendars, and Gmail/iCloud email capture, weekly AI-generated insights that compare older memories for changes or conflicts, and a dashboard with list/graph views, backup/restore, and seven tunable retrieval parameters. v2.3 added a context-aware home screen, customizable AI model choices per function, and Italian localization. Distribution is unusually accessible: a desktop app for Mac and Windows handles setup with no terminal work, while developers can deploy with one click via Cloudflare's deploy button or run the Worker manually. The intended audience is power users and professionals who use multiple AI tools daily and want a private, portable memory layer they fully control.

**Product Description Text**:
> Graph-R1: Towards Agentic GraphRAG Framework via End-to-end Reinforcement Learning

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Graph-R1 addresses the limitation of existing GraphRAG methods, where the disconnect between graph-structured knowledge and language model reasoning hinders retrieval performance. It introduces an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework that enhances the reasoning-on-graph capabilities of large language models by constructing a knowledge hypergraph via n-ary relation extraction and employing explicit reward feedback. The framework drives an iterative "think–generate query–retrieve subgraph–rethink" reasoning cycle, enabling LLMs to flexibly integrate structured graph knowledge into their answers. Experiments evaluate the approach on six GraphRAG benchmark datasets (2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, Musique, NQ, PopQA, TriviaQA) across multiple RL algorithms (GRPO, REINFORCE++, PPO) and LLM scales (e.g., Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct), with demonstrated applicability to knowledge-intensive domains such as healthcare, finance, and law. The codebase, built on PyTorch 2.4.0 and FlashAttention, provides end-to-end pipelines for data preprocessing, knowledge hypergraph construction, retrieval server setup, and distributed RL training requiring 4×48GB GPUs. Researchers and engineers working on GraphRAG, retrieval-augmented generation, or agentic LLM reasoning pipelines will find this a useful reference implementation for ICML 2026 work by Luo et al.

**Product Description Text**:
> A pure-Python context management layer for LLM systems — retrieval, re-ranking, memory decay, and token-budget enforcement in one pipeline.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> context-engine is a pure-Python library that addresses what standard RAG pipelines neglect — assembling, prioritizing, and fitting context under real token constraints before it reaches an LLM. It unifies five components into a single `build()` pipeline: a Retriever supporting keyword, TF-IDF, and hybrid embedding modes; a tag-weighted re-ranker; a Memory module with exponential decay, auto-importance scoring, and deduplication; a Compressor offering truncate, sentence, or extractive query-aware strategies; and a TokenBudget enforcer that allocates slots across system prompts, history, and documents. The library is aimed at developers building multi-turn conversational LLM systems, production RAG applications with large or noisy knowledge bases, and anyone operating under tight context-window limits where retrieval quality alone is insufficient. Its stack is intentionally minimal — Python standard library plus NumPy as the only hard dependency, with `sentence-transformers` as an optional addition that enables hybrid retrieval (falling back to TF-IDF without it). Latency on a 5-document knowledge base runs roughly 92ms for a full pipeline build, making it suitable for applications that can tolerate sub-100ms context-assembly overhead in exchange for structured budget enforcement and decaying memory across turns.

A new "memory" stacklet in v0.3 builds an Obsidian-compatible family wiki by curating documents, notes, and voice memos, with a local AI engine (Whisper, oMLX, Piper) running on Apple Silicon GPUs for transcription, document classification, and natural-language Q&A within chat. Designed for tech-curious parents who value privacy, it requires only a Mac with Apple Silicon, Homebrew, and OrbStack—no Linux or Docker expertise needed—and gets a full family server running in roughly twenty minutes from clone to deployment.


#### 165. [LLM-RAG-Architecture](https://github.com/matt-bentley/LLM-RAG-Architecture/tree/main) (`matt-bentley/LLM-RAG-Architecture`)
- **Official URL**: [https://github.com/matt-bentley/LLM-RAG-Architecture/tree/main](https://github.com/matt-bentley/LLM-RAG-Architecture/tree/main)
- **Primary Language**: `C#` | **Stars**: `★ 73` | **License**: `MIT`
- **Catalog Provenance**: Channel: *Cooly* | Video: *Cooly's Chrome Links* | Published: *2026-09-02*
- **Attached Keywords**: `linux, retrieval-augmented-generation, ai, rag, llm, framework`
- **GitHub Topics**: `ai, ai-assistant, dotnet, python, rag`

**Product Description Text**:
> Production-grade Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture using Open Source components

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> A production-grade Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system built on open-source components, enabling accurate, citation-backed Q&A over document corpora. It tackles the limitations of standalone LLMs—including hallucinations and outdated knowledge—by grounding responses in retrieved source material. The architecture combines dense vector search with BM25 sparse retrieval, fuses results via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, and reranks outputs using a cross-encoder (BAAI/bge-reranker-base) for higher precision. Built around a .NET 10 console application orchestrated by Semantic Kernel, it supports multiple LLM providers (Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, Ollama), uses Qdrant as the vector database, and leverages a Python FastAPI embedding service (BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5). PDF ingestion is handled with multiple extraction strategies, and an interactive chat interface enables natural-language control over indexing and querying. The system is ideal for developers and architects building enterprise-grade document intelligence, knowledge management, or domain-specific AI assistants where accuracy, transparency, and extensibility are critical.


#### 166. [brain-map-skill](https://github.com/vladignatyev/brain-map-skill) (`vladignatyev/brain-map-skill`)

- **Catalog Provenance**: Channel: *Github Awesome* | Video: *GitHub Trending Skill #4: self-learning-skills, lazyskills, guard-skills, agent-skills, edict-agent* | Published: *2026-07-14*
- **Attached Keywords**: `frontend, data-visualization, python, knowledge-graph, markdown`

**Product Description Text**:
> Brain-Map-Skill is an interactive HTML knowledge map generator that turns a folder of Markdown notes (such as an Obsidian vault or gbrain export) into a themed force graph with a growth timeline. The resulting visualization shows how topics and notes are connected and how the user's knowledge has expanded over time. The project ships with a prebuilt demo so users can see the result before generating their own. Brain-Map-Skill is aimed at note-takers, researchers, and learners who want a visual map of their Markdown corpus.

Alan Turing discussed the centrality of learning as early as 1950, in his classic paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence".[120] In 1956, at the original Dartmouth AI summer conference, Ray Solomonoff wrote a report on unsupervised probabilistic machine learning: "An Inductive Inference Machine".[121]  This is a form of Tom Mitchell's widely quoted definition of machine learning: "A computer program is set to learn from an experience E with respect to some task T and some performance measure P if its performance on T as measured by P improves with experience E." > Diagram→code through a deterministic rules gate: the AI proposes, 50 rules verify, only valid architecture lands. Try it: app.solarch.dev

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Solarch is an AI-assisted architecture design tool that generates valid software diagrams from natural language prompts by routing every AI proposal through a deterministic Rules Engine before it lands on the canvas. It solves the problem of LLM hallucinations in code generation by enforcing 40 whitelist rules, 7 anti-patterns, and 3 conditional checks, ensuring illegal connections (such as frontends talking directly to databases) are rejected and the AI self-corrects until the graph is clean. The platform features 21 node families (controllers, services, repositories, tables, DTOs, queues) and 16 semantic edges, backed by a vector-native Neo4j database with local 384-d multilingual embeddings and GraphRAG over a canonical pattern library. Validated diagrams convert deterministically into NestJS scaffolds, with optional Surgical AI for method bodies, while a type-safe pipeline (Zod → OpenAPI → openapi-fetch) keeps the contract honest from database to button. Developers, software architects, and engineering teams seeking reliable AI-driven system design will find it especially valuable, as will anyone wanting self-hostable architecture tooling without Docker dependencies, accessible instantly through app.solarch.dev.

Notes are organized through unlimited nested folders, pinning, and a soft-delete trash with auto-purge, while a versioning system captures snapshots every five minutes (up to 50 per note) for change tracking and recovery. It indexes repositories once using tree-sitter for symbol extraction and a bundled ONNX model for embeddings, then exposes four tools over MCP: a symbol graph (callers, callees, inheritance, dead code), hybrid semantic search, blast-radius analysis with risk scoring, and convention detection that learns how a team actually writes code. The tool targets AI-assisted development workflows where accurate dependency reasoning, impact analysis, and stylistic consistency matter more than raw text search. **Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Graphify solves the problem of navigating and understanding large, multi-format codebases by converting them into a queryable knowledge graph instead of forcing developers to grep through files manually. By invoking the `/graphify` skill in AI coding assistants like Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or Gemini CLI, users can map an entire project—including source code, documentation, SQL schemas, configuration files, and PDFs—into a structured graph that can be explored visually or queried programmatically.

The tool relies on local, deterministic AST parsing via tree-sitter across roughly 40 programming languages, meaning code analysis requires no LLM calls and no data leaves the user's machine. Each edge in the resulting graph is explicitly tagged as either `EXTRACTED` (directly present in the source) or `INFERRED` (resolved through graph traversal), giving users clear visibility into provenance. Output includes an interactive `graph.html` viewer, a `GRAPH_REPORT.md` summary highlighting key concepts and surprising connections, and a portable `graph.json` file for later querying, path-finding, and explanation. Unlike vector-based memory systems, Graphify builds a true traversable graph with community detection (Leiden algorithm), cross-file relationship resolution (`calls`, `imports`, `inherits`, `mixes_in`), and integration of rationale comments and ADR references.

It is aimed at developers, architects, and engineering teams working with unfamiliar or sprawling codebases who nee

Instead of a human manually tweaking code, an AI agent autonomously modifies train.py—the single file containing the GPT model, Muon+AdamW optimizer, and training loop—runs a fixed 5-minute training budget, evaluates the result via validation bits-per-byte (val_bpb), and keeps or discards the change in a continuous experimental loop. It is designed for ML researchers and engineers experimenting with agentic AI workflows who want to explore autonomous research loops on a self-contained PyTorch stack requiring only a single NVIDIA GPU and Python 3.10+. The minimal codebase consists of just prepare.py (fixed data prep and utilities) and train.py (the agent's editable surface), deliberately constrained for comparability across hardware and reviewable diffs.

Users upload source materials and describe their prediction goals in natural language; the system extracts entities, generates personas with independent personalities and long-term memory (via Zep and GraphRAG), and runs thousands of autonomous agents through social interactions to simulate emergent behaviors, producing a detailed prediction report and a deeply interactive sandbox.

The engine supports both serious applications (policy rehearsal, public relations testing, financial and political event forecasting) and creative use cases (e.g., simulating the lost ending of *Dream of the Red Chamber*).

Key features include a "God's-eye view" for injecting variables at runtime, dual-platform parallel simulation, dynamic temporal memory updates, and the ability to chat directly with simulated agents post-run.

The platform serves decision-makers, analysts, researchers, and creators seeking exploratory forecasting, backed by the OASIS open-source simulation framework from CAMEL-AI and incubated by Shanda Group.

Built on Python 3.11+, Node.js 18+, and a React frontend, it integrates any OpenAI-SDK-compatible LLM (Qwen-plus recommended) and supports deployment via source code or Docker.

GBrain targets individual developers wanting a personal knowledge agent, YC-style teams needing scoped shared institutional memory (each user gets a permissioned slice with zero cross-leak fuzz-tested across all read paths), and AI agent builders wiring it in as a supercharged retrieval layer for Claude Code or Codex. **Product Description Text**:
> Context window optimization for AI coding agents. Sandboxes tool output, 98% reduction. 12 platforms

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> Context Mode is an MCP server that tackles the context window bloat problem faced by AI coding agents, where raw tool outputs (Playwright snapshots, GitHub issues, log files) can consume 40% or more of the available context within minutes. It achieves a 98% reduction in token usage by sandboxing tool outputs, keeping raw data out of the model context while preserving access to computed results. Session continuity is maintained through an SQLite-backed event store indexed with FTS5 and queried via BM25, so agents retain awareness of file edits, tasks, and user decisions across compaction cycles without re-dumping history into context. The "Think in Code" paradigm replaces dozens of file-read tool calls with a single sandboxed script that outputs only the relevant result, and routing enforcement is applied automatically across 17 supported platforms via MCP plus hook integrations. It is licensed under ELv2, distributed as an npm package and Claude Code plugin, and targets engineering teams using AI coding assistants in environments such as Claude Code, Cursor, and other MCP-compatible clients.

It addresses common scaling problems in conversational AI—system prompts that break down under complexity and routed graph architectures that become fragile when handling natural, non-linear interactions. **Product Description Text**:
> TurboVec high-performance vector processing engine. TurboVec is an open-source vector processing library designed for fast similarity search and vector operations

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> turbovec is a vector index built on Google Research's TurboQuant algorithm, compressing embeddings to 2-bit or 4-bit with near-optimal distortion and no training phase. A Rust core exposes the index through Python bindings, and hand-written SIMD kernels (NEON SDOT/SMMLA on ARM, AVX-512 VNNI and `vpermb` on x86) let it beat FAISS `IndexPQFastScan` across measured configurations while shrinking a 31 GB float32 corpus to roughly 4 GB. Online ingest means vectors are indexed immediately on `add`, and `sync(path)` persists only incremental changes with a single fsync per call, enabling crash-safe durability without rebuilding the index. Search supports id-based allowlists or slot bitmasks filtered directly inside the SIMD kernel, making it well suited for hybrid retrieval pipelines that combine dense reranking with external candidate selection. It targets developers building privacy-sensitive, low-latency, or memory-constrained RAG systems who need a fully local vector store, with optional integrations for LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, and Agno.

It parses repositories into a Tree-sitter AST stored as a SQLite graph of functions, classes, imports, and call/dependency edges, then computes the minimal set of files an AI assistant must read by tracing "blast radius" from any change. A single `install` command auto-detects and configures 15+ supported platforms (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, Zed, Continue, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, and others), injects graph-aware rules, and exposes MCP tools so assistants query the graph instead of scanning the whole repo. Incremental updates run in seconds via file hooks and watch mode using SHA-256 diffing, and benchmarked results show up to ~71x token reduction on real codebases (e.g., flask: 143,594 → 2,196 tokens). Distributed as a pip-installable Python 3.10+ package, it targets developers and teams using AI coding assistants who want faster, cheaper, and more accurate reviews on large repositories.

The core is agent-agnostic Python tooling and TypeScript/Three.js runtime, licensed under Apache 2.0, aimed at developers who need lightweight, inspectable 3D reconstructions that can be edited and animated rather than opaque downloaded models.

AI researchers, browser-agent developers, and engineers looking to extend existing coding agents like Claude Code or Codex with web capabilities will find it useful. Built on Python, Playwright, httpx, pydantic, and typer, it deliberately avoids multi-agent orchestration, graph engines, or plugin layers.

**Product Description Text**:
> Harness engineering is the practice of improving coding-agent output by shaping the environment around a fixed model—specifically the context and tools it receives—rather than altering the agent itself. This anthology from Ryan Lopopolo argues that the private, changing "process data" beneath any organization's work (its operational state, ontology, quality bar, exception history, and authority relationships) cannot be presumed to exist in general model weights, so it must be made retrievable to the agent at runtime. The repository packages that thesis into three deliverables: an `AGENTS.md` and `docs/` thesis index that route an agent to relevant arguments and proofs, `playbooks/` for applied tasks, and a `sources/` library of cited talks, tweets, and papers that anchor the framing. A central design principle is that the repository itself should teach the agent—converting nonfunctional requirements (reliability, security, performance, maintainability, risk posture) into executable constraints, examples, and checks embedded in the codebase. Because work is iterative, the harness makes organizational judgment cumulative: accepted work, corrections, and failures feed back as context, boundaries, and tools for future runs, allowing coherence to compound across agent-maintained artifacts. The intended audience is engineering leaders and platform teams building agent-first workflows who need a concrete methodology and reference bundle for turning organizational knowledge into agen

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> dsRAG is a high-performance retrieval engine designed for unstructured data, particularly excelling at complex queries over dense, lengthy documents like financial reports, legal filings, and academic papers. It addresses the limitations of vanilla RAG systems—which struggle with questions requiring synthesis across multiple text sections—by introducing three core techniques: semantic sectioning, AutoContext, and Relevant Segment Extraction (RSE). Semantic sectioning uses an LLM to partition documents into coherent segments with descriptive titles, while AutoContext prepends document- and section-level metadata to chunks before embedding, dramatically improving retrieval precision. Relevant Segment Extraction clusters related chunks at query time and intelligently reassembles them into longer, contextually complete segments tailored to the question. The library supports multiple vector databases including Faiss, Chroma, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus, and Pinecone, and is installable via pip with optional dependency groups. Benchmarks demonstrate substantial accuracy gains, achieving 96.6% on FinanceBench compared to 32% for vanilla RAG, and an average score improvement from 4.72 to 8.42 on the KITE benchmark. It is well-suited for AI engineers and developers building production-grade RAG applications where retrieval quality over complex document corpora is critical.

It solves the problem of accurately identifying and categorizing ROM files by storing metadata, checksums, and serial numbers in clrmamepro `.dat` format files, which are compiled into RetroArch's proprietary `.rdb` format for efficient runtime use. Key features include ROM validation through checksum matching, standardized game naming, thumbnail association, category-based browsing ("Explore"), and per-game information views, all powered by a key field system that uses CRC checksums for smaller files and serial numbers for disc-based games. The repository also bundles plain-text `.cht` cheat code files organized by system, enabling users to apply cheats directly within RetroArch. It serves a community of retro gaming enthusiasts, developers of libretro cores, and contributors who maintain metadata sourced from third-party projects like No-Intro, Redump, MAME, and TOSEC. The technology stack relies on plain-text DAT definitions transformed into binary `.rdb` files via build scripts, with RetroArch performing byte-array scans to extract serials from disc-based media, avoiding the computational cost of hashing large files.

**Product Description Text**:
> To speed up Long-context LLMs' inference, approximate and dynamic sparse calculate the attention, which reduces inference latency by up to 10x for pre-filling on an A100 while maintaining accuracy.

**Extended Synopsis / Feature Analysis**:
> MInference addresses the computational bottleneck of processing million-token contexts in large language models by exploiting the dynamic sparse nature of attention patterns during the pre-filling stage. It identifies static sparse patterns for each attention head offline, then approximates sparse indices online using optimized custom kernels, achieving up to 10x pre-filling speedup on A100 GPUs while preserving accuracy. The repository has evolved into a comprehensive long-context inference suite, now incorporating SCBench (a KV cache-centric evaluation benchmark accepted at ICLR'25) and MMInference (modality-aware sparse attention for vision-language models at ICML'25). It supports a broad ecosystem of efficient methods spanning the entire KV cache lifecycle—including compression techniques (StreamingLLM, SnapKV, PyramidKV), retrieval approaches (CacheBlend, RetrievalAttention), and alternative sparse attention variants (xAttention, FlexPrefill)—with kernels integrated into production frameworks like vLLM and SGLang, yielding up to 15x speedup at 1M context length. Researchers and engineers working with long-context LLMs (LLaMA-3, Qwen2.5-1M, GLM-4-1M) and VLMs would use this tool to accelerate inference without sacrificing quality. The implementation is built on PyTorch with Triton kernels and FlashAttention-2, and installs via `pip install minference`.

- **Attached Keywords**: `ai-agents, python, cli, agent, context-management, memory, knowledge-base`

**Product Description Text**:
> OptMem is a lightweight, permanent memory system designed for AI coding agents like Claude Code. It solves the statelessness problem that forces agents to lose context between sessions, compactions, model switches, and vendor changes by giving them a single, append-only log of long-term facts. The system consists of a single dependency-free Python 3 script (`memo`) installed via curl, plus a 426-token Markdown prompt that any agent pastes into its `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`. From there, agents run `memo wake` at session start to read their memory and `memo note "<line>"` whenever they learn something worth keeping, with merges handled one at a time in command output rather than via background processes. Storage uses fixed-width records so position equals identity, enabling O(1) lookups that scale to a million memories (608 MB) with wake times of 0.03 seconds. Summaries form a binary tree that can be navigated with `memo zoom <a>-<b>` and rebuilt from the log alone, making the cache fully reconstructible. Search is regex-based (`memo recall`), bad summaries can be dropped with `memo forget`, and the entire memory directory can be redirected via `$MEMORY_DIR` to sync across machines or version-control. The target users are developers running long-lived AI agent workflows who need continuity without maintaining complex infrastructure or external databases.

**Product Description Text**:
> Trace File Lineage is a Python tool that reconstructs where files came from, guides AI coding agents on where to place new outputs, and reports what each task actually produced. It works in two complementary modes: retrospective analysis that ranks candidate origins for existing files by parsing code, parsing notebooks, reading document metadata, and searching Git history; and verified provenance recorded automatically when wrapping a command with `lineage run`. Every answer is labelled with one of five assurance tiers — `verified`, `strong-candidate`, `candidate`, `weak-signal`, or `insufficient` — so guesses are never mistaken for proof. Key features include an interactive offline graph (`lineage open`) that distinguishes solid proof arrows from dashed guess arrows, Mermaid export, an `agent-run` view that nests changed files into a readable tree, `impact` and `stale` analysis for inputs, and a `layout --suggest` command that recommends conventional output paths or admits when no convention exists. Built primarily for Python 3.11–3.14 and Jupyter workflows (with first-class parsing of Pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, PIL, and pathlib), it also handles Office documents, PDFs, images, and EPUB, while deliberately staying shallow on JavaScript/TypeScript and other languages. All scanning, storage, and analysis happen locally — nothing is uploaded, secrets are skipped automatically, and only command summaries and changed-file lists are retained from agent runs.

**Product Description Text**:
> Slopo is a command-line tool that detects non-exact code duplication across codebases using embedding models, focusing on similar snippets that are hard to spot manually because they sit far apart in different modules or files. It works by generating vector embeddings for each code unit, then identifying pairs whose embeddings are close, producing ranked clusters of potentially duplicated code. Results are designed to feed into AI coding agents, which can confirm true duplicates, mark false positives as ignored via a persistent ignore file, and drive refactoring. The tool supports ten languages including Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, Java, Kotlin, C#, Go, Rust, PHP, and Elixir, and integrates with any LiteLLM-compatible embedding provider (such as Voyage AI) or local servers like Ollama. Slopo persists state in a local SQLite database, supports incremental re-indexing, and generates Markdown reports sorted by similarity and codebase distance, making it well suited for development teams seeking to surface hidden code duplication for refactoring.


#### 208. [minisqlite](https://github.com/cursor/minisqlite) (`cursor/minisqlite`)

- **Attached Keywords**: `sqlite, database, tools, rust`

**Product Description Text**:
> minisqlite is a from-scratch reimplementation of SQLite written in Rust, providing a full SQL database engine with parser, query planner and executor, transactions, and a storage engine that reads and writes SQLite's official on-disk file format. It exposes a deliberately minimal public API consisting of a single `Connection` type with four methods (`open`, `open_in_memory`, `execute`, `query`), plus the `Value`, `Row`, and `Error` types, making it suitable for embedding in Rust applications that need SQLite-compatible persistence without linking against the C library. The implementation spans roughly 200,000 lines across 14 layered crates covering the SQL dialect (including joins, CTEs, window functions, upserts, generated columns, triggers, and foreign keys), about 90 built-in functions, ~20 PRAGMAs, WAL and rollback-journal modes, and ~5,650 tests. It uses only one external dependency (`elsa`, for the page cache) and contains no `unsafe` code in library code, making it attractive for projects that prioritize memory safety and a small dependency surface. The intended audience includes systems programmers, database researchers, and developers who need a verifiable, auditable, format-compatible SQL engine in pure Rust.

**Product Description Text**:
> Sakura Crossing is a fully explorable 3D neighbourhood in Three.js that renders to look like a hand-painted 2D anime background, solving the challenge of producing a cel-shaded look without any image assets. Every sign, lantern, and shop fascia is drawn at runtime with Canvas2D, while the "anime" aesthetic comes from four layered techniques: quantised toon lighting with a hue-shifted shadow ramp, a screen-space second-difference depth ink pass, inverted-hull outlines on key props, and a two-light setup with split-tone colour grading. The world is a small planet centred on a Japanese level crossing and grows outward to include a shopping street, shrine, high school, residential lanes, a festival ground, and a railway that loops the entire globe; the scene is deliberately unpopulated, letting detritus and signage carry the atmosphere. Twenty-two interactables respond to the `E` key, including nineteen vending machines that dispense cans and a relay box that calls a train (which otherwise arrives every 35–45 seconds), and a coral-painted e-bike can be summoned for fast traversal. Built with three.js and Vite as the only dependencies, it runs on any Node 18+ setup and targets developers and graphics enthusiasts interested in non-photorealistic rendering pipelines for anime-style real-time scenes.

**Product Description Text**:
> Understory provides a self-wiring, plain-markdown memory layer for AI agents, solving the problem of persistent, structured knowledge management that remains human-readable and version-controlled. It stores every learned fact as a markdown concept with YAML frontmatter following the Open Knowledge Format (OKF) spec, automatically cross-linking them into a living knowledge graph where concepts are sized by connections and orphans are visually flagged. The system exposes this memory through three interfaces: an MCP server (with `memory_query`, `memory_add`, `memory_update`, `memory_status`, and `memory_maintain` tools), a web UI featuring an Obsidian-style force-directed graph viewer with replayable query-path traces, and a CLI for smoke testing. A core design principle separates concerns by enforcing bundle conformance (frontmatter validation, index regeneration, sandboxed paths) in deterministic code while delegating content decisions to the LLM, ensuring the storage layer remains valid regardless of model output. The stack is a pnpm monorepo with `packages/core` handling the OKF bundle layer and agent tool loop via the Vercel AI SDK, `packages/server` providing Express-based MCP streamable-HTTP, REST, and streaming chat endpoints, and `packages/web` delivering a React + Tailwind interface. It targets AI agent developers using MCP-compatible clients like Claude Code who want durable, inspectable memory that works with any OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible provider, including fu

- **Attached Keywords**: `design, svg, frontend, javascript`

**Product Description Text**:
> liquid-glass is a single-file, dependency-free JavaScript module that brings Apple's liquid-glass aesthetic to the web by making translucent panels actually bend the content behind them at their edges. It solves the problem of convincingly simulating refractive glass in CSS, where standard `backdrop-filter: blur()` produces only a flat frosted look. The technique uses an SVG `feDisplacementMap` filter driven by a canvas-generated displacement map (RGB ramps encoding X/Y offsets, neutralized in the interior so refraction is confined to a rim band), with three staggered per-channel passes combined via `feBlend` to produce a faint chromatic-aberration fringe. Real refraction is supported in Chromium browsers, while Safari and Firefox automatically fall back to a configurable frosted blur. Frontend developers building marketing sites, design portfolios, or app-style UIs can drop it onto any DOM element, tune parameters like `scale`, `chroma`, `border`, `mapBlur`, and `blur` via a simple options object, and rely on automatic resize handling plus a `destroy()` method for clean integration with frameworks like React.

Their identity is checked and their billing process reviewed.' versions:   free-pro-team: '*' ---  ### About verified creators  A verified creator is an organization that {% data variables.product.company_short %} has checked. Anyone can share their apps with other users on {% data variables.product.prodname_marketplace %} but only organizations that are verified by {% data variables.product.company_short %} can sell apps. For more information about organizations, see "[About organizations](/github/setting-up-and-managing-organizations-and-teams/about-organizations)."  The verification process aims to protect users. For example, it verifies the seller's identity, checks that their {% data variables.product.product_name %} organization is set up securely, and that they can be contacted for support.   After passing the verification checks, any apps that the organization lists on {% data variables.product.prodname_marketplace %} are shown with a verified creator badge {% octicon "verified" aria-label="Verified creator badge" %}. The organization can now add paid plans to any of their apps. Each app with a paid plan also goes through a financial onboarding process to check that it's set up to handle billing correctly.  ![verified creator badges](/assets/images/marketplace/marketplace_verified_creator_badges_apps.png)  In addition to the verified creator badge, you'll also see badges for unverified and verified apps. These apps were published using the old method for verifying individual apps.  ![Green verified and grey unverified badge](/assets/images/marketplace/marketplace_verified_badges.png)  For information on finding apps to use, see "[Searching {% data variables.product.prodname_marketplace %}](/github/searching-for-information-on-github/searching-github-marketplace)."  ### About the verification process  The first time you request verification for a listing of one of your apps, you will enter the verification process.  An onboarding expert will guide you through the process. This includes checking:  - Profile information - The basic profile information is populated accurately and appropriately. - Security - The organization has enabled two-factor authentication. - Verified domain - The organization has verified the domain of the site URL. - Purchase webhook event - The event is handled correctly by the app.  When your organization is verified, all your apps are shown with a verified creator badge. You are now able to offer paid plans for any of your apps.   For more information about the requirements for listing an app on {% data variables.product.prodname_marketplace %}, see "[Requirements for listing an app on {% data variables.product.prodname_marketplace %}](/marketplace/getting-started/requirements-for-listing-an-app-on-github-marketplace/)."  {% data reusables.marketplace.app-transfer-to-org-for-verification %} For information on how to do this, see: "[Submitting your listing for publication](/developers/github-marketplace/submitting-your-listing-for-publication#transferring-an-app-to-an-organization-before-you-submit)."  {% note %}  **Note:** This verification process for apps replaces the previous process where individual apps were verified. The current process is similar to the verification process for actions. If you have apps that were verified under the old process, these will not be affected by the changes. The {% data variables.product.prodname_marketplace %} team will contact you with details of how to migrate to organization-based verification.  {% endnote %}   12  content/developers/github-marketplace/billing-customers.md  @@ -13,17 +13,17 @@ versions:  ### Understanding the billing cycle  Customers can choose a monthly or yearly billing cycle when they purchase your app. All changes customers make to the billing cycle and plan selection will trigger a `marketplace_purchase` event. Once you've submitted your app, one of the {% data variables.product.prodname_marketplace %} onboarding specialists will reach out to you with more information about the onboarding process, and review your app to ensure it meets these requirements: ### Requirements for all {% data variables.product.prodname_marketplace %} listings  ### User experience All listings on {% data variables.product.prodname_marketplace %} should be for tools that provide value to the {% data variables.product.product_name %} community. When you submit your listing for publication, you must read and accept the terms of the "[{% data variables.product.prodname_marketplace %} Developer Agreement](/articles/github-marketplace-developer-agreement/)."  - {% data variables.product.prodname_github_app %}s should have a minimum of 100 installations. - {% data variables.product.prodname_oauth_app %}s should have a minimum of 200 users. #### User experience requirements for all apps  All listings should meet the following requirements, regardless of whether they are for a free or paid app.  - Listings must not actively persuade users away from {% data variables.product.product_name %}. - Listings must include valid contact information for the publisher. - Listings must have a relevant description of the application. - Listings must specify a pricing plan. - Apps must provide value to customers and integrate with the platform in some way beyond authentication. - Apps must be publicly available in {% data variables.product.prodname_marketplace %} and cannot be in beta or available by invite only. - Apps cannot actively persuade users away from {% data variables.product.product_name %}. - Marketing materials for the app must accurately represent the app's behavior. - Apps must include links to user-facing documentation that describe how to set up and use the app. - When a customer purchases an app and GitHub redirects them to the app's installation URL, the app must begin the OAuth flow immediately. For details, see "[Handling new purchases and free trials](/marketplace/integrating-with-the-github-marketplace-api/handling-new-purchases-and-free-trials/#step-3-authorization)." - Apps must have webhook events set up to notify the publisher of any plan changes or cancellations using the {% data variables.product.prodname_marketplace %} API. They should be able to view and manage those accounts separately.
